blocks.text: This is treated in detail by Rosenmüller (Bibl. Alterth. vol. 4, Part 2, p. 188 ff.) and Winer (Bibl. R. W. s.v. Einhorn). Most later investigations follow that second view, and probably with the most justification, since not only does the Arabic رئم [riʾm], or رئم [riʾm], denote a species of gazelle, but the Talmud also has ארוילא, or אורוילא for ראם (Sebachim 113b), and the former word corresponds all too closely to the Arabic غزال [ghazāl]; the North African Arabs even [p. 150] pronounce the word Rgazál.

However, we have here only to examine the Talmudic view of ראם, and in this regard we must above all emphasize one principal point, namely the fabulous size which the Talmud attributes to the animal in many passages. As the extreme of size it is set in contrast to the nits of lice. Sabbat 107b and frequently elsewhere it says: “God tends and nourishes everything, from the קרני ראמים to the ביצי כינים.”

We shall come back to these names. It is further said: the ראם is so large that it could not enter Noah's ark; it had to be tied to the ark by its horn, so that it could keep its nose free and breathe (Sebachim 113b). In another passage there is fabulous talk of the size of an אורזילא בר יומא (an אורזילא one day old, so reads Samuel

רש"בם —; the Tosephot, on the other hand, read: אורזילא דבר ראימא “young אורזילא”) (B. batra 74b); in this passage the biblical חנינים הגרולים (sea monsters) are also rendered by ארזילי רימא, which Samuel in turn explains by ראמים שבים. Thus throughout, size is the characteristic feature attributed to the animal by the Talmud*), whereas the Bible ascribes to it agility (Ps. 29, 6), wildness (Job 39, 9), and strength (Deut. 33, 17) as its characteristic. If we now take that point given on the Talmudic side as the starting point of the investigation, then one must most probably think of the unicorn, not only because, owing to its being so little known, it was the most suitable subject for fable, but chiefly on account of its size. The Antilope Oryx at most equals the ox in size and is well known in Egypt, but especially in inner Africa; this latter animal therefore fits the Talmudic passages in question too poorly. That size, however, was considered above all is evident from the Tosephot (Sebachim 113b; s.v. אורזילא), according to which in some places the buffalo (בופלש §. 159) was also called ראם, which surely happened only because the animal, on account of its size, in which it surpasses the ox, seemed suited to the name ראם; the Tosephot at the same time remark, however, that the buffalo cannot be the actual ראם, since it falls far short of the supposed size of the latter*). [p. 151]
Raschi (A. Sara 3b) too can translate ראם only as “a large animal”; one may therefore probably assume that the Talmud understood by ראם only the unicorn.

Onkelos uses it to translate the biblical דישן (Deut. 14, 5), which belongs to the clean animals; accordingly it must have had cloven hooves, which is indeed said to be the case with the unicorn (Rosenmüller ibid. p. 194). Its tallow (§. 92) is therefore also eaten (Tosephot Sebachim ibid.). Cf. §. 22.

We have only to press the matter of the name. Usually the animal is called ראם, or רימא (Sebachim ibid.), whereas in Sabbat 107b and in the parallel passage A. Sara 3b it is called קרני ראמים, which, however, is already biblical and a poetic phrase (Deut. 33, 17; Ps. 22, 22); likewise Oppian (in his poem on hunting with hounds: Κυνηγετικά [Kynēgetika] 2, v. 474) names the black horn of the oryx: Κερόεντα μέτωπα [keroenta metōpa]; evidently the Talmud designates with קרני not the plurality of horns but of animals, just as in German “Einhörner” means only several animals of the uni-

corn kind. The Talmud uses the plural of the unicorn as of the nits: ביצי כינים, for which otherwise אינבא is used; the אינבא arises from the ביצה כינים (louse egg, §. 451), so that that expression too is used of the mass, or plurality, of the nits. We must not, however, conceal that in Midr. Jalk. Schim. part 2, §. 845 קרנותיו occurs in reference to the Reem; but our task is only to establish the view of the Talmud, and the reading of the Midrash should certainly be emended.
In three passages (Chulin 60a Sabbat 28b and A. Sara 8a) it is said: “The ox which Adam, the first man, had sacrificed had only one horn on its forehead.”

This animal cannot be identical with the unicorn treated in the preceding article, if only for the reason that the latter belongs to the class of wild animals and thus, as a species unfit for sacrifice, would certainly not have been substituted by the Talmud as that first sacrifice. In that [p. 152] second Talmudic passage the sex of the one-horned ox is even especially emphasized. Now already Pliny (h. n. 8, 21, 30 and 31) reports that one- and three-horned oxen exist in Ethiopia, and expresses himself thus: In India et boves solidis ungulis, unicornes “In India there are also solid-hoofed, one-horned oxen”, and we should probably think here of this Indian ox, although, to be sure, on account of its uncloven hooves it could not have been sacrificed according to later legal prescription. In any case it is more readily to be assumed that Adam (we of course separate legend from natural history) would far rather have sacrificed the easily caught and subdued ox than that fabulous, huge and unconquerable unicorn. The Talmud too, drawing on Ps. 69, 32, calls it שור פר, which fits that Indian ox better. It is therefore an error when D. Oppenheim (in Frankel's Monatsschrift für Ges. u. Wissensch. d. Judenth. vol. 4, p. 281 ff.) identifies our animal with the unicorn, just as he also erred in his interpretation of the קרס (§. 146).
